Lataste’s viper (Vipera latastei) is a relatively small-bodied viperid endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and northern Maghreb. Neonates emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs measuring approximately 16 centimeters [Lb = approximately 16 centimeters] in total length, a modest size that reflects the constraints of yolk-dependent embryogenesis within a cleidoic egg. This value is consistent with the small litter sizes typical of the genus, as a single clutch may contain between two and thirteen offspring [N_R_i = single clutch may contain between two and thirteen offspring]. When maintained at a constant 24 °C [T = 24 °C], a temperature that approximates the thermal optimum for vitellogenesis in Mediterranean vipers, females typically produce only a single clutch every three years [F_R_i = single clutch every three years], a remarkably slow reproductive tempo imposed by the high energetic cost of gestation in a cool, seasonal climate. This low reproductive frequency, combined with the small size at birth, positions Vipera latastei as a classic K-selected strategist among European reptiles.

As individuals progress through the juvenile stage and approach sexual maturation, they exhibit a steady increase in body size. Puberty is attained when males and females reach a total length of approximately 35 centimeters [Lp = approximately 35 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to the onset of gonadal activation and the first copulation attempts. This length at sexual maturity is relatively modest compared to many congeneric vipers, reflecting the species’ adaptation to the resource-limited Mediterranean ecosystems it inhabits. Field records indicate that the age at which this length is reached varies geographically, with individuals in cooler, montane populations taking longer to accumulate the somatic reserves necessary for reproductive activation. Once the 35-centimeter mark (35 centimeters) [Lp = 35 centimeters] is surpassed, the transition from immature organism to reproductively viable adult is rapid, and gravid females are regularly encountered during the late spring and early summer months following successful cloacal copulation.

The ultimate size that reproductively active adults of Vipera latastei can achieve has been documented through both field surveys and museum specimen series. Maximum body size is typically expressed as snout–vent length, and the largest recorded individuals attain an ultimate SVL of 58 centimeters [Li = 58 centimeters], although total length including the tail may reach up to 72 centimeters. This asymptotic body length is associated with a corresponding maximum adult wet weight of 196 grams [Wwi = 196 grams], a value recorded from field surveys of Iberian populations. Such a mass is moderate for a viperid of this body plan and reflects a life history strategy that prioritizes the production of relatively large, well-provisioned offspring over the attainment of extreme adult body dimensions. The combination of a 58-centimeter SVL (58 centimeters) [Li = 58 centimeters] and a 196-gram ultimate mass (196 grams) [Wwi = 196 grams] suggests a robust, moderately elongated body shape typical of terrestrial ambush predators.

The maximum longevity observed in this species has been determined from long-term mark–recapture studies conducted at several protected sites in northern Portugal. The oldest documented individual persisted for 5,110 days (5110 days) [am = 5110 days] when maintained at the thermal conditions typical of the species’ active season, specifically 24 °C [T = 24 °C], which is equivalent to approximately 14 years. This lifespan is notably longer than that of many similarly sized European reptiles and underscores the slow pace of life that characterizes this viper. The extended period likely facilitates multiple reproductive events over an adult’s lifetime, compensating for the extremely low annual reproductive output imposed by the triennial clutch cycle. At 24 °C [T = 24 °C], captive individuals have been known to survive for comparable durations, confirming that the species possesses a naturally low senescence rate independent of environmental stressors.

In a comparative context, Vipera latastei occupies an interesting position among the Palearctic viperid fauna. Its pubertal total length of 35 centimeters [Lp = 35 centimeters] is similar to that of the closely related Vipera aspis, although the latter attains a slightly smaller ultimate body size. The combination of a 196-gram maximum adult mass (196 grams) [Wwi = 196 grams] and a triennial reproductive cycle with 2 to 13 offspring per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 13 offspring per clutch] places this species at the slow end of the fast–slow continuum of life-history variation among vipers. At 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of approximately 13 offspring every 3 years [Ri = approximately 13 offspring every 3 years] underscores how effectively environmental temperatures constrain reproductive output in temperate-zone ectotherms. Understanding how climate change may alter the frequency of these already infrequent breeding events remains a critical question for the conservation of this endemic Iberian viperid.
